questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Using the Pythagorean Trigonometric Identity
questions.worked_solution:
We use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x=1
$$

Using the above, we compute the given integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{4}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x({cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x\cdot 1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Using the Pythagorean Trigonometric Identity
questions.worked_solution:
We use a variation of the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x=1\,⟹\,{cos}^{2}⁡x=1-{sin}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Using the above, we rewrite the denominator and calculate the resulting integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \frac{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{1-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x})\text{d}x \\  & =\int ({sec}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x+\operatorname{sec}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Recall  ${cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x=1.$ 
Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-1}=\frac{1}{-{sin}^{2}⁡x}=-{csc}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /6}^{5\pi /6}\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x-1}\,\text{d}x & =-{\int }_{\pi /6}^{5\pi /6}{csc}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡x{|}_{\pi /6}^{5\pi /6} \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡\frac{5\pi }{6}-\operatorname{cot}⁡\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =-\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{3} \\  & =-2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Using the Secant-Tangent Identity
questions.worked_solution:
We are using the identity

$$
{tan}^{2}⁡x+1={sec}^{2}⁡x\,⟹\,{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x-1.
$$

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\frac{3(\operatorname{sec}⁡x-1)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡x+1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\frac{({sec}^{2}⁡x-1)}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\frac{{tan}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =3\operatorname{sec}⁡x\,{|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3} \\  & =3\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-3\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =3\cdot 2-3\cdot \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =6-2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we select the identity that contains a ${tan}^{2}⁡x$ term. So we can use the identity 

$$
1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Using the above, we compute the given integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }({cos}^{3}⁡x+{tan}^{2}⁡x{cos}^{3}⁡x)\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{3}⁡x(1+{tan}^{2}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{3}⁡x{sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{cos}^{3}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡0 \\  & =0-0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}\frac{3({cot}^{2}⁡x+1)}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x\operatorname{csc}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =3{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}\frac{{cot}^{2}⁡x+1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x\operatorname{csc}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x\operatorname{csc}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{csc}⁡x}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3\operatorname{csc}⁡x\,{|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3} \\  & =-3\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})+3\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =-3\cdot \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}+3\cdot \sqrt{2} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}-2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}

questions.worked_solution:
In this case, we have to use the identity

$$
1+{cot}^{2}⁡x={csc}^{2}⁡x\,⟹\,{csc}^{2}⁡x-{cot}^{2}⁡x=1.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{e-1}}\frac{x}{{csc}^{2}⁡x+{x}^{2}-{cot}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{e-1}}\frac{x}{({csc}^{2}⁡x-{cot}^{2}⁡x)+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{e-1}}\frac{x}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{x}^{2})\,{|}_{1}^{\sqrt{e-1}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+(\sqrt{e-1})^{2})-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+(1)^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+e-1)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(e)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(2) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(1)-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{2} \\  & =\frac{1-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

From the identity $1+{cot}^{2}⁡\theta ={csc}^{2}⁡\theta ,$ with $\theta =5x-2,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}1+{cot}^{2}⁡(5x-2)={csc}^{2}⁡(5x-2).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{{cot}^{2}⁡(5x-2)\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x-2)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x-2)}\,\text{d}x & = \\ \int \frac{1}{[{cot}^{2}⁡(5x-2)+1]\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x-2)}\,\text{d}x & = \\ \int \frac{1}{{csc}^{2}⁡(5x-2)\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x-2)}\,\text{d}x & = \\ \int \frac{{sin}^{2}⁡(5x-2)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x-2)}\,\text{d}x & = \\ \int \operatorname{sin}⁡(5x-2)\text{d}x & = \\ -\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x-2)+C & .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
From the identity $1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta $ with $\theta =x+\frac{\pi }{4},$ we get 

$$
1-{cos}^{2}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{4})={sin}^{2}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{4}).
$$

Substituting the above into our integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{1-{cos}^{2}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{4})}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{4})}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{csc}^{2}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{4})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡(x+\frac{\pi }{4})\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{\pi }{4})-[-\operatorname{cot}⁡(0+\frac{\pi }{4})] \\  & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{cot}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =-0+1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We use a variation of the Pythagorean identity:

$$
\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad  \cos^2 x = 1-\sin^2 x.
$$

Using the above, we rewrite the denominator and calculate the resulting integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we select the identity that contains a $\tan^2{x}$ term. So we can use the identity 

$$
1+\tan^2x =\sec^2x.
$$

Rearranging the above identity gives

$$
\tan^2 x =\sec^2 x -1.
$$

Using the above, we compute the given integral as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
		\int \tan^2 x \, \textrm{d}x&=\int \left(\sec^2 x -1\right ) \, \textrm{d}x\
				&=\tan x -x+C.	
	}
$$

In this case, we have to use the identity  $1+\cot^2x =\csc^2 x.$ Rearranging this gives

$$
\eqalign{
		\cot^2 x &=\csc^2 x -1.
}
$$

Substituting this into our integral gives

$$
\eqalign{
		\int \left(5\cot^2 x -x^2\right) \, \textrm{d}x&=\int \bigg(5\left(\csc^2 x -1 \right) -x^2\bigg) \, \textrm{d}x\
				&=\int \left(5\csc^2 x -5 -x^2\right ) \, \textrm{d}x\
				&=-5\cot x -5x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}+C.	
	}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
From the identity  $1+\tan^2 \theta =\sec^2 \theta$ with $\theta = 3x,$ we get 

$$
\eqalign{
		1+\tan^2 (3x) &=\sec^2 (3x)\
		\tan^2 (3x) &=\sec^2 (3x) -1.
}
$$

Substituting the above into our integral gives

$$
\eqalign{
		\int 2\tan^2 (3x) \, \textrm{d}x&= 2\int \tan^2 (3x) \, \textrm{d}x\
                                                                &= 2\int \left(\sec^2 (3x) -1\right ) \, \textrm{d}x\
                                                                 &= 2\left(\int \sec^2 (3x)\, \textrm{d}x -\int1 \, \textrm{d}x\right)\
				                                &= 2\left( \dfrac{1}{3}\tan (3x) -x\right)+C\
                                                                 &= 	\dfrac{2}{3}\tan (3x) -2x+C.
	}
$$
